title: Unit 4e - File I/O Introduction
summary: Title slide introducing the File I/O unit in CS 103, covering reading from and writing to files using C++ file streams. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 4e on File I/O in the CS 103 course. File I/O (Input/Output) covers how C++ programs can read data from files stored on disk and write data to files. This unit introduces the ifstream and ofstream classes from the fstream library, which provide file access using the same stream interface as cin and cout.
notes_text: File I/O is essential for programs that need to persist data beyond program execution or process large amounts of input data that would be impractical to type manually.

title: getline() Member Function and Lines of Text
summary: Explains that cin stops at whitespace, and introduces cin.getline() to read entire lines including spaces, stopping only at newline characters.
main_text: The cin input stream stops reading at whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines). If you want to read a whole line of text including spaces, use cin.getline(). It will read spaces and tabs but STOPS at the newline character. The syntax is cin.getline(char *buffer, int max_chars), which reads max_chars-1 characters leaving space for the null character. The code example demonstrates: a char array mytext[80] is declared, then cin.getline(mytext, 80) reads a full name including the space. Compare this with cin >> mytext which would only read the first word. The program then searches for a space character to find where the last name starts. When the user enters 'Tommy Trojan', the program correctly identifies that the last name starts at index 6.
notes_text: The getline function is critical when reading input that contains spaces, such as full names, addresses, or sentences. Without getline, cin >> would only capture the first word. The max_chars parameter prevents buffer overflow by limiting how many characters are read.

title: Input Stream Error Checking
summary: Shows how to use cin.fail() to detect input errors when cin receives data that cannot be converted to the expected type, like entering text for an int.
main_text: We can check errors when cin receives unexpected data that cannot be converted to the given type. Use the function fail() member function (i.e. cin.fail()) which returns true if anything went wrong opening or reading data in from the file. Once fail() returns true, it will continue to return true from then on until you perform cin.clear(). For now in CS103, the approach is to print an error and exit. The code example declares int x, y and prompts for an integer. If the user enters 'abc' instead of an integer, cin >> x fails. Checking cin.fail() detects this error and prints 'Error: I said enter an int!' before exiting with return 1. Importantly, once cin enters a fail state, subsequent reads (cin >> y) will also fail regardless of input, as the fail state persists until cin.clear() is called.
notes_text: The fail() function is essential for robust input handling. Without checking for errors, a program might continue with uninitialized or incorrect values. The sticky nature of the fail state (persisting until clear() is called) is important to understand to avoid cascading errors.

title: Simple File I/O Using Filestream Objects Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to the topic of getting data into and out of files stored on disk using ifstream and ofstream objects.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the main topic: Simple File I/O Using Filestream Objects. The subtitle explains the focus: getting data into and out of files stored on disk using ifstream and ofstream objects. These are the C++ standard library classes that enable programs to read from and write to files on the filesystem.
notes_text: The ifstream (input file stream) and ofstream (output file stream) classes mirror the behavior of cin and cout but operate on files instead of the keyboard and screen.

title: File I/O Intro - Input Methods
summary: Introduces File I/O as a third input method alongside cin and command line arguments, with two approaches: file streams and I/O redirection.
main_text: What methods does a user have to provide a program input? Previously covered: cin for interactive keyboard input and command line arguments (argc, argv). Now a third method is introduced: File I/O, which means accessing data stored in files. The primary methods for a program to read/write files are: File streams, which are the main subject of this lecture and use ifstream/ofstream objects to directly read/write files, and I/O Redirection, which is the subject of a later lecture and uses the OS to redirect input and output from cin and cout to files instead of the keyboard and monitor.
notes_text: File I/O is by far the most common way real-world programs handle data. Almost every application reads configuration files, processes data files, or saves output to files. Understanding file streams is fundamental to practical programming.

title: Important Fact - Data Must Be Read Into Variables
summary: Emphasizes that to operate on file data, you must first read it into program variables using ifstream, as the processor cannot access disk files directly.
main_text: For your program to operate on data in a file, you must read it into a variable. Everything covered subsequently is simply how to get data from a file into a variable, or take data from a variable and save it to a file. The diagram shows the data flow: a file data.txt on DISK contains '15 21 hello'. The program ./app1 uses an ifstream object to read from the disk file into program variables. After reading, the program variables x=15 and y=21 are available in memory for the program to use. This illustrates the fundamental concept that the processor works with data in RAM (variables), not directly with files on disk.
notes_text: This is a foundational concept: files are on disk, but programs operate on data in memory (variables). The ifstream acts as a bridge between disk storage and program memory, converting file contents into usable variable values.

images.description: Diagram showing data flow from a disk file (data.txt containing '15 21 hello') through an ifstream object down into program variables (x=15, y=21) in the ./app1 program. Arrows show the downward flow from disk to memory.

title: File I/O Overview - File Streams vs I/O Redirection
summary: Compares two file I/O methods: file streams (ifstream/ofstream) that directly access files, and I/O redirection that routes cin/cout to files via the OS.
main_text: There are two methods for file I/O. File streams (ifstream and ofstream) are part of the C++ library and perform file I/O directly through a cin- and cout-like interface. You create an ifstream object, open a file, and use >> to read data just like cin. I/O redirection is covered later in the semester. With I/O redirection, the OS reads or writes data to/from a file by controlling cin and cout. The program just performs normal cin and cout commands, and the OS redirects them. The command line syntax is: $ ./app1 < data.txt which redirects the contents of data.txt to cin. The left diagram shows the file stream approach: data flows from disk file dat1.txt through an ifstream object into program variables. The right diagram shows I/O redirection: the OS intercepts cin and feeds file data through it, so the program uses cin >> x >> y as normal.
notes_text: File streams give the programmer explicit control over which files to read/write and when. I/O redirection is simpler but less flexible since the program cannot open multiple files or switch between files during execution. In practice, file streams are used much more often.

images.description: Two parallel diagrams comparing file I/O methods. Left: ifstream reads from dat1.txt on disk through an ifstream object into variables x=15, y=21. Right: I/O redirection via '$ ./app1 < data.txt' feeds file data through cin into the same variables, with the OS handling the redirection.

title: Disk Access and Memory Architecture
summary: Explains that all code and data resides in RAM, the processor cannot access disk directly, and file streams abstract OS routines for disk access.
main_text: All code and data (variables) resides in RAM. The processor can ONLY talk directly to RAM (memory) and cannot access files on disk directly. Files on your disk require special OS routines to access their data. The OS provides routines to perform the translation between disk storage and memory. C++ provides file streams to abstract those OS routines and help to: take data from a file and input it to your variables, or take your variables and write their values to a file. The diagram shows the system architecture: the processor connects to RAM which contains Code, Globals, Heap, and Stack sections. Separately, data files (.mpg, .txt, .docx) are stored on disk as binary data (110010101001...). The OS mediates between RAM and disk storage.
notes_text: Understanding the memory hierarchy is important for appreciating why file I/O requires explicit operations. Unlike variables which are instantly accessible in RAM, file data must be transferred from the much slower disk storage through OS system calls, which the fstream library abstracts away.

images.description: System architecture diagram showing: processor chip connected to RAM (containing Code, Globals, Heap, Stack sections), and separate disk storage containing data files (.mpg, .txt, .docx) as binary data. Arrows indicate data flow between processor, RAM, and disk.

title: Recall: I/O Streams
summary: Reviews how cin and cout use stream buffers to temporarily store I/O data, and explains how the same stream abstraction applies to files.
main_text: C++ and the OS use the notion of streams to temporarily store (buffer) data to be input or output, and then use the cin and cout objects (from the <iostream> library) to access those streams. These objects have internal data members and member functions. While cin has a stream that receives input from the keyboard and cout has a stream that outputs to the terminal, the same stream abstraction could be applied to files. The diagram shows two flows: for input, the keyboard sends data through the OS to an input stream memory (stdin) containing bytes like '7', '5', then cin extracts data via cin >> x. For output, cout sends text like 'It was the\nbest of times.' to an output stream memory (stdout), which the OS then displays on the monitor.
notes_text: The stream abstraction is a powerful design pattern. By using the same interface (>> and <<) for both console and file I/O, C++ makes it easy to switch between reading from keyboard and reading from file with minimal code changes. This is polymorphism in action.

images.description: Two flow diagrams showing I/O streams. Top: keyboard through OS to input stream memory (stdin) containing '7 5 y ...', then cin extracts data. Bottom: cout sends 'It was the' to output stream memory (stdout) containing characters, then OS displays on monitor.

title: File Streams - ifstream and ofstream
summary: Introduces ifstream as the file counterpart to cin and ofstream as the counterpart to cout, with code examples showing reading from and writing to files.
main_text: C++ leverages the SAME interface that cin and cout provide to: read data IN from a file (like cin, but data comes from a file not the keyboard) and write data OUT to a file (like cout, but data goes to a file not the terminal). The counterpart to cin is an ifstream object, and the counterpart to cout is an ofstream object. The reading example shows: include <fstream>, create ifstream ifile("dat1.txt"), then use ifile >> x to read an integer from the file, just like cin >> x. The input stream memory buffers the file data. The writing example shows: create ofstream ofile("dat2.txt"), then use ofile << "Hi there" << std::endl to write to the file, just like cout. The output stream buffers data before the OS writes it to dat2.txt on disk. Both examples call .close() when done.
notes_text: The key insight is that ifstream and ofstream use the exact same >> and << operators as cin and cout. This means all the formatting, error checking (fail()), and getline operations work identically with file streams. The only difference is where the data comes from or goes to.

images.description: Two parallel diagrams. Left: disk file dat1.txt (containing '75 yes 23 no') flows through OS to input stream memory, then ifstream object reads into variables x=15, y=21. Right: ofstream writes 'Hi there\n' to output stream memory, then OS writes to dat2.txt on disk.

title: Input and Output Streams Summary
summary: Summarizes that file streams provide the same capabilities as cin/cout but for files, using >> with ifstream and << with ofstream.
main_text: To summarize, there are other types of input and output streams other than cin and cout. File streams give the same capabilities as cin and cout, except data is read/written from/to a file on the hard drive. Everything you do with cin using the >> operator you can now use with an ifstream to access data from a file. Everything you do with cout using the << operator you can now use with an ofstream to output data to a file. The lecture will continue learning more about the >> operator in the context of cin and cout, but students should realize it will apply to other streams (file streams) as well.
notes_text: This symmetry between console I/O and file I/O is a deliberate design choice in C++. It means students only need to learn one set of I/O operations, and the same code patterns work for both interactive and file-based programs.

title: Starting File I/O - Open, Read/Write, Close
summary: Outlines the three-step pattern for file I/O: open the file with ifstream/ofstream, read or write data, then close the file when done.
main_text: Just like a document or image editor allows two operations on files, C++ file I/O follows the same pattern. To read info from a file (like the 'Open' command): use an ifstream object to open the file, read data from the file using the >> operator or getline, and close it when you're done. To write info to a file (like the 'Save As' command): use an ofstream object to create/open the file, write data to the file using the << operator, and close it when you're done. This open-read/write-close pattern is the fundamental workflow for all file I/O operations.
notes_text: Always close file streams when you are done with them. While the destructor will close them automatically when the object goes out of scope, explicitly closing files is good practice because it ensures data is flushed to disk and system resources are released promptly.

title: Two Kinds of Files: Binary and Text
summary: Distinguishes text files (sequences of ASCII characters) from binary files (raw binary data), noting that this unit focuses exclusively on text file I/O.
main_text: We conceive of files as streams (1D arrays) of data. Files are broken into two types based on how they represent the given information. Text files: a file is just a large sequence of ASCII characters, where every piece of data is just a byte. Each digit or character is stored separately in ASCII. Binary files: data in the file is just bits that can be retrieved in different size chunks (4-byte int, 8-byte double, etc.). For example, storing the number 172 in a file: in Text format, it would store 3 ASCII characters '1','7','2' (ASCII codes 49, 55, 50) requiring 3 bytes, where the key is each digit is stored separately in ASCII. In Binary format, if 172 was in an int variable, we could store it as 4 bytes in binary rather than separate ASCII characters. In this unit, the focus is only on text file I/O.
notes_text: Text files are human-readable when opened in a text editor, while binary files appear as gibberish. Text files are larger for numeric data (each digit takes a byte) but are portable and easy to debug. Binary files are more compact and faster to read/write but require knowing the exact format to interpret.

title: Text File I/O Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to the detailed coverage of text file I/O operations.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the detailed coverage of Text File I/O. The following slides will cover the specific syntax and usage patterns for reading from and writing to text files using ifstream and ofstream objects, including error checking and reading lines of text.
notes_text: Text file I/O is the most common form of file I/O in introductory programming courses and is sufficient for most data processing tasks.

title: Text File I/O - ifstream
summary: Shows complete ifstream usage: include fstream, create ifstream with filename, check fail() for open errors, use >> to read data, and check fail() after reads.
main_text: To read from a text file, you must include <fstream>. Use an ifstream object/variable for reading a file. It can do anything cin can do. You must open the file, usually by specifying the filename when you create the ifstream: ifstream ifile("input.txt"). Use the >> operator, .fail(), and .getline() with the ifstream object just as you would on cin, but realize operations are happening on data from the file. The code example shows: declare int x and double y, create ifstream ifile("input.txt"), immediately check if(ifile.fail()) to verify the file opened successfully. If it fails, print an error and return 1. Then read data with ifile >> x >> y, and check ifile.fail() again to verify the data was read correctly. The input file input.txt contains '5 -3.5', so x gets 5 and y gets -3.5.
notes_text: Always check fail() after opening a file and after reading data. Common reasons for open failure: file does not exist, wrong path, insufficient permissions. Common reasons for read failure: file contains data in wrong format (e.g., text where a number is expected) or end of file reached.

images.description: Code example showing complete ifstream usage with input.txt file icon containing '5 -3.5'. The code creates an ifstream, checks for open errors, reads an int and double, and checks for read errors.

title: Text File I/O - ofstream
summary: Shows complete ofstream usage for writing to files: include fstream, create ofstream with filename, use << operator, and close all file streams when done.
main_text: To write to a text file, you must include <fstream>. Use an ofstream object/variable for writing to a file. It can do anything cout can do. Use the << operator, I/O manipulators, etc. on the stream but realize operations are happening on data going to the file. Close all filestreams using the .close() member function when done. The complete code example shows both reading and writing: first create ifstream ifile("input.txt") and check for errors, then read ifile >> x >> y. Next create ofstream ofile("output.txt"), then write formatted output with ofile << "Int from file is " << x << endl and ofile << "Double from file is " << y << endl. Finally close both streams with ifile.close() and ofile.close(). The input file input.txt contains '5 -3.5' and the output file output.txt will contain 'Int from file is 5' and 'Double from file is -3.5'.
notes_text: When you create an ofstream with a filename, it creates a new file or overwrites an existing file. To append to a file instead, use ofstream ofile("output.txt", ios::app). Always close files to ensure all buffered data is written to disk.

images.description: File icons showing input.txt containing '5 -3.5' and output.txt containing 'Int from file is 5' and 'Double from file is -3.5', demonstrating the complete read-process-write workflow.

title: Getting Lines of Text from Files
summary: Shows how to use ifile.getline() to read entire lines from files, including a loop pattern to read all lines until end of file.
main_text: Recall that using the >> operator to get an input string of text (char* or char[] variable passed to cin) implicitly stops at the first whitespace. To get a whole line of text (including spaces), use getline: cin.getline(char *buf, int bufsize) for console input, or ifile.getline(char *buf, int bufsize) for file input. It reads max of bufsize-1 characters (including newline), reads and discards the newline, and places a NULL char at the end of the string. The code example reads all lines from a file and adds line numbers. It creates char myline[100] and int i=1, opens ifstream ifile("input.txt"), checks for errors, then uses ifile.getline(myline, 100) followed by a while(!ifile.fail()) loop that prints the line number and text, then reads the next line. The input file contains three lines: 'The fox jumped over the log.', 'The bear ate some honey.', 'The CS student solved a hard problem.' The output numbers each line 1:, 2:, 3:.
notes_text: The pattern of reading before the loop and reading again at the end of the loop body is called a 'priming read' pattern. It ensures fail() is checked after each read attempt. An alternative is while(ifile.getline(myline, 100)) which combines the read and check.

images.description: Input file input.txt containing three lines of text with visible newline characters, and the program output showing the same lines prefixed with line numbers 1:, 2:, 3:.
labels: The fox jumped over the log.
The CS student solved a hard problem.

title: Activity - File I/O Exercises
summary: Closing slide directing students to practice with File I/O exercises.
main_text: This slide directs students to complete File I/O exercises to practice the concepts covered in this unit. The exercises reinforce creating ifstream and ofstream objects, reading data from files, writing data to files, error checking with fail(), and reading lines of text with getline.
notes_text: Hands-on practice with file I/O is essential because the open-read/write-close pattern and error checking are skills that require repetition to internalize.
